# What the revival changed in the team's Fortress

This part gives the departures of revived Fortress from the team's Fortress, and from what you expect from Java, Scala, Haskell or Julia. The team left three forms that disagree: the specification, walk with the interpreter's library, and the compiled path with the compiler's library. The rules below resolve them. Read the part whole, after `SKILL.md`, before work.

Each bold rule states the rule of this tree. A sentence that names a POSITIONS entry (P-N) states a decision of the curator. Build on a sentence without one, but do not cite it as a decision. Question a rule only on new evidence (`SKILL.md`, "When to explore"). Most rules follow the team's later type papers (`Papers/`) over the specification's early text (P-26; `exploring.md`). The Working Draft is the unrevised specification, in `Specification-1.0-frozen/`. Where a rule changed the specification, Appendix I keeps the original text (`specification.md`).

A sentence that cites a ledger row states a known departure of one path from a bold rule. A fix can change it, so do not assert it as correct in a test. A sentence that opens "Until the switch-over" states a limit of the compiler's library. The limit ends when the compiled path moves onto the interpreter's library, so do not fix it in the compiler's prelude (`compiler.md`). If a change is not here, search FACTS and POSITIONS (`records.md`) before you call a disagreement a conflict. An old note, a team test and your training can be right about the team's walk and wrong here: the number types do not nest, fixed-width arithmetic does not wrap, and walk converts arguments.

## Dispatch and overloading

**Overloads may differ in their static parameters (P-45).** An example is `ident[\T extends Shape\](x: T): T` beside `ident[\T extends Round\](x: T): T`. The Working Draft forbids such pairs. A declaration's declared domain is the set of argument types that its declared parameter types accept at some instance within its bounds: every `Shape` for the first `ident`. The checker applies the overloading rules of `SKILL.md` to declared domains. The more specific declaration's return type must be a subtype of the other's at every instance, not at one only.

**Where a declaration has static parameters, exclusion is read over the whole tuple of parameter types (P-152).** By the exclusion rule, a value of both domains has one instance of each generic type at each position, so those instances' static arguments are equal. The domains exclude where these equalities cannot hold together, or where some position excludes at the instance that they force. So `o[\T\](x: P[\T\], b: Box[\T\])` beside `o[\T\](x: Q[\T\], b: Box[\T\])`, with `P[\T\] excludes { Q[\T\] }`, is valid. Both paths refuse a pair where the equalities leave a static parameter free, as `o[\T, U\](x: Q[\U\], b: Box[\T\])` beside the first `o`: nothing ties `U` to `T`. In its test of whether two domains exclude each other, the checker puts the meet of a static parameter's declared bounds in the parameter's place where the parameter is a whole parameter type, an element of a tuple or a member of an intersection or union (P-157). Inside a static argument, as `T` in `Box[\T\]`, the parameter stays.

**Walk chooses by declared parameter types, never by the order of the declarations.** It compares declared domains where one lies strictly inside the other. Otherwise it compares the instances that the call makes. It infers a dotted generic method's static arguments from the arguments' run-time types, as for a generic function. A trait's generic method called with an argument outside a bound fails with "Cannot unify".

**Walk's load check is not the verdict of these rules.** It refuses some valid pairs and loads some invalid ones, and the checker differs from it on others. Before you change code to pass walk's check, or take its acceptance as proof, find the case in `interpreter.md`, "What walk checks": a case that cites a ledger row is a departure of walk. For example, walk compares two functional methods of a generic trait or object on their declared domains only at a call (row 780).

**Two functional methods with equivalent parameter types are duplicates, wherever `self` stands.** So the checker refuses `f(self, y: S)` beside `f(x: S, self)` in a trait `S`. Abstract declarations count:

- both paths refuse an abstract and a concrete method with the same parameter types in one trait;
- both paths refuse an object that inherits an abstract functional method from one trait and its body from another, unless the object declares the method itself (P-149). The Scala language accepts it.

The Meet Rule asks for a declaration that covers the meet of two overloads that neither exclude each other nor nest (`SKILL.md`, "Fortress as a language"). An abstract functional method also counts for it. So the checker refuses `h(self): ZZ32` in a trait `S` beside a top-level `h(x: String): ZZ32`: nothing covers the meet of `S` and `String`. Likewise, a program's trait that declares its own functional `+` overlaps the library's `+` between an array and a number, because a type can extend both the trait and `Number`, which has no `comprises` clause (P-160). Declare the trait `excludes { Number }`, or make it exclude arrays, `excludes { HasRank }`. Or declare the `+` in an object, not in a trait: an object excludes every trait that it does not extend, because no other type can extend it. Otherwise walk refuses the program at load: "fails the Meet Rule". The checker refuses such a pair in one component, but accepts it against the library's `+` (row 918). Give a trait with its own functional `-`, `MIN` or `MAX` the same fix: the library declares these in the same form.

## Traits and objects

**The compiled checker applies the exclusion rule (P-43, P-97).** It refuses a type that extends two instantiations of one generic trait. Walk does not apply the rule: it runs such a type, and refuses overloads on two instantiations, as `g(b: Tg[\3\])` beside `g(b: Tg[\4\])`, because it does not read them as excluding (row 416). The specification marks the Working Draft's examples that break the rule "Not allowed": do not copy them.

**A `comprises` clause speaks of values (P-60).** Every value of the trait that declares it is a value of a listed type. So a generic trait need not be listed if every type below it is below a listed type, as `Integral[\I\]` below `AnyIntegral`. A Java `permits` list names each direct subtype; this clause need not. Read so, several declarations can together cover the meet of two overloads. At load, walk checks extenders only against the clauses of the program's main component (row 551).

**`override` widens.** An `override` overrides an inherited declaration only where the inherited parameter types are strictly narrower than its own. To replace an inherited declaration at its own parameter types, declare it again without `override`. An `override` in a trait also overrides in every type below it. The checker checks that an overriding return type is a subtype. Walk refuses at load an `override` that, by this rule, overrides nothing, so a Java-style `override` in the library stops every program. Two departures: the checker accepts such an `override` (row 653), and the code generator refuses every `override` modifier (row 650).

**An object defines an inherited abstract method by bodies that together cover its parameter types (P-147).** It needs one body at those types, or several narrower bodies that cover them, with `comprises` clauses read. Walk refuses at load an object without static parameters that leaves one uncovered. Walk skips this check for a generic object (row 665). Walk stops its search for a cover at limits that `interpreter.md` gives, and the checker at the same limits. The checker refuses a cover by several bodies where the abstract or a covering method has static parameters (row 725).

**In a self-typed trait the checker types `self` as the trait met with the implementing type.** A trait `T` is self-typed if both conditions hold:

- `T` has no `comprises` clause, or one that lists only `...`;
- `T` has a parameter `X` bounded by `T` itself, as `trait T[\X extends T[\X\]\]` (P-146), or by a self-typed trait `U[\X\]` that `T` extends, as `trait T[\X extends U[\X\]\] extends U[\X\]`.

In `T`'s bodies, `self` has the intersection type of `T[\X\]` and `X`. So `floor(self): I = self` in `Integral[\I extends Integral[\I\]\]` is valid without a cast. The checker refuses a type that extends `T[\A\]` and is not an `A`. A compiled body of `T` that returns `self` fails the JVM's verification when its class loads (row 695).

When the checker applies the overloading rules to a method of `T`, `self` has the type `T[\X\]`, except in its test of whether two domains exclude each other. There `self` has the intersection type of `T[\X\]` and `X` (P-157). With this reading and the bounds that the test reads ("Dispatch and overloading"), the library's generic `+` and `-` between an array and a number are valid beside `AdditiveGroup`'s own. Walk reads `self` in the same way, so it loads such a pair in the library and in a program's own component. Walk's load check, which is not the verdict ("Dispatch and overloading"), still refuses the pair in two cases:

- `T` is self-typed only through another self-typed trait that it extends;
- `T`'s method has static parameters of its own.

**An indexed type's index parameter is bounded by `Index` (P-156).** An indexed type is a type whose values `a[i]` subscripts, such as an array. Its index parameter is the static parameter that gives the type of `i`. In the library, and in your own generic over such a type, write `I extends Index`. Walk runs the code without the bound. The checker refuses it when it checks against the interpreter's library, as the count stage does (`compiler.md`). Of the integer types, only `ZZ32` extends `Index`, and `Range` excludes `Index`. To the checker a numeral is an `IntLiteral`, which is no `Index`. So it refuses `f(3)` for `f(x: Index)`. Walk takes it (row 364). Pass a `ZZ32` value there instead. `a[3]` stays valid, because an array indexed by `ZZ32` takes a `ZZ32`. The Working Draft lets no trait type hold a tuple, but here a tuple whose element types are all `Index` types is an `Index`. So `m[i, j]` passes the pair `(i, j)` as one index. `Index` extends only `Any`, so such a tuple is still no `Object`. The empty tuple `()` is no `Index`. A function over `Index` and one over a tuple of `Index` types do not exclude each other. Until the switch-over, the compiler's prelude declares no `Index`, so a program that names it does not compile: write the bound only in code that runs under walk or is checked against the interpreter's library. Two departures:

- the checker refuses a tuple expression at a parameter of type `Index`, but takes one at a parameter of type `I`, where `I extends Index` (row 805);
- walk loads a function over `Index` beside one over a pair whose element types neither lie below `Index` nor exclude it (row 806).

**Pairs and triples are ordered only where each element type extends `StandardPartialOrder`.** This holds for `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=` and `CMP`. Walk refuses another element type at the call, also where earlier elements decide, as `(1,()) < (2,())`. It also refuses numbers of two run-time types at one position, as `(1,2) < (1,2.5)` (row 511). Unordered deciding elements give `false`, or `Unordered` for `CMP`. The checker orders a `List[\E\]` only where `E extends StandardTotalOrder[\E\]`, so a list of `RR64` has no order there (P-154). Walk orders every list (row 774). A list's `=` stays element by element.

**Where a type declares no `=`, `=` is strict equivalence, `SEQV` (P-168).** Strict equivalence is the operator `≣` (STRICTLY EQUIVALENT TO), written `SEQV` or `===` in ASCII. The operator `≡` (IDENTICAL TO, `EQV` or `EQUIV`) is a different one: logical equivalence on booleans. The interpreter's library declares it for no type, and walk stops on it (row 184): write `a <-> b`. The library's `=` over `Any` answers `a SEQV b`. `SEQV` follows the specification on both paths:

- values of different types are never equivalent;
- a value object is equivalent field by field, a tuple element by element, an integer, a character or a boolean by its value, and a float by its bits;
- a reference object, a string among them, is equivalent only to itself;
- a function is equivalent to itself, but may be found unequal to another that behaves the same.

So for a value object `V` without its own `=`, `V(s) = V(t)` is `false` where `s` and `t` are equal strings made by two computations. Under walk, each evaluation of a string literal makes a new string, unlike Java, which interns literals. So `"ab" SEQV "ab"` and `V("ab") = V("ab")` are `false`. The library declares `=` on pairs and triples only, so `(s, 1, 2, 3) = (t, 1, 2, 3)` is `false` too. Both `false` answers are the rule's: assert them as correct. Under walk a float numeral is a `FloatLiteral`, a type of its own, so it is not equivalent to a computed `RR64` (`interpreter.md`, "How walk evaluates a program"). To compare by content, give the value object an `=`, or compare the parts. A string's `=` compares text. Under walk, `≠` (`=/=` or `NE`) and `assert(x, y, msg)` reach a type's own `=` only if the type extends a library trait that declares `=`, such as `Equality` (row 807). Otherwise write `assert(x = y, msg)`. Until the switch-over, the compiler's library declares no `=` over `Any` and none on tuples. Its own `≣`, declared as `===`, compares strings and `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `RR32` and `RR64` by `=`, not by bits or identity (row 908).

## Static parameters, `where` clauses and sizes

**A type parameter that a call does not fix takes its bound, not Scala's `Nothing` (P-48).** The checker takes the intersection of its upper bounds, narrowed by the expected type. Under walk, a parameter whose bound names itself stays open, printed `OPEN`, as in `BoxU[\OPEN\]`. Every value passes `OPEN` itself. Where walk compares overloads, a type that holds `OPEN` admits only what it admits at `Bottom`: beside `pick(x: Any)`, `pick(x: (T,T))` takes no `(1, 2)`. Walk still gives `Bottom` to these parameters:

- one with two bounds, neither below the other (row 591);
- one that an argument bounds only from above, with a bound that names another static parameter (row 612);
- one that only the result of a function expression without a return type fixes (row 587).

**Only the checker gives a call written as an argument the enclosing call's context (P-51).** If the enclosing call fails as written, the checker types the inner call again against each declaration's parameter type. So `takesBox64(mk())` compiles for `mk[\T\](): BoxT[\T\]`. Walk gives an argument no expected type, so there `mk()` takes its bound (row 705). Under walk, write `mk[\ZZ64\]()`.

**Three `where` forms are built (P-151).** Conditional extension is an `extends` entry with a `where` clause that binds no variable and states only constraints `T extends SomeTrait`. The type extends the parent only where they hold, as `List[\E\]` extends `LexicographicOrder[\List[\E\],E\] where { E extends StandardTotalOrder[\E\] }`. The other two forms:

- a condition of a function or method on its own static parameters, or of a method on its trait's, checked at a call;
- a type variable of a `where` clause in a `comprises` clause, as `AnyList comprises List[\E\] where [\E\]`.

The checker reads an `extends` entry with any other `where` clause as unconditional, without a message. Walk and the compiled runtime apply a conditional extension at every instance (row 774). Walk runs a dotted call that breaks a method's condition (row 777). The code generator accepts a declaration's own `where` clause but emits no code for it, so the compiled runtime does not check it. A compiled call of a function or method whose own clause introduces a `where`-clause variable, as `where [\nat n\]` does, dies at run time (row 867). `compiler.md` gives the checker's gaps.

**Sizes are compared by their written form (P-55).** The checker checks sizes against their kind, and the runtime carries each as a descriptor. Two sizes are equal when they are written alike after numeral arithmetic: `2 3` is `6`, but `s0 s1` is not `s1 s0`. A static parameter is not known to differ from a numeral, so in `typecase N[\b0\] of N[\0\] => ...` the arm is reachable. The checker refuses a size power above the exponent 4096, except of 0, 1 or -1. Walk refuses a negative exponent. The class loader computes a size without checking its kind, and stops on a negative exponent with a Java exception (row 675).

**A size known only at run time comes from `reflect` in `NatReflect.fsi`.** Its value, a `NatParam`, passed where the object type `N[\n\]` is expected, binds `n` at the call. Such a call does not run compiled yet. Until the switch-over, compiled programs do not link `NatReflect`, which is part of the interpreter's library. After the switch-over, such a call still fails, for a second reason. `NatParam` is declared `comprises { N[\n\] } where [\nat n\]`, so its `comprises` clause lists a type at a `where`-clause size. A compiled call fails the JVM's verification if it passes a value of such a trait where a listed type is expected (row 307). This holds for a program's own trait too.

## Numbers

**The number types are flat siblings (P-43).** The record calls this choice route A. Route C is the way not chosen: a checker rule under which the number types could nest again. The record still calls the number and order traits "the tower". That word does not mean that they nest.

**Under walk a numeral has a run-time class.** The checker types an integer numeral as `IntLiteral`, a sibling under `Number` that converts to the integer types, `QQ` and `RR64` (P-76). Walk gives a numeral the class `Int`, `Long` or `BigNum` by its value. These classes stand for `ZZ32`, `ZZ64` and `ZZ`, but a generic instantiates at the class. Walk prints these classes as `ZZ32`, `ZZ64` and `ZZ`, also inside static arguments, so a printed type does not show the instance: `Cell(3)` prints `Cell[\ZZ32\]` but is a `Cell[\Int\]`, and no `Cell[\ZZ32\]` (row 364). Where you need a `Cell[\ZZ32\]`, write `Cell[\ZZ32\](3)`. Walk's own error messages say `Int`. Walk answers `IntLiteral`'s arithmetic as a `ZZ32` (row 578). The library's factories `array1` and `array2` give a `Vector` or `Matrix` only at the eight number types, not at a user subtype of `Number`. Elsewhere they give a plain array, whose `+` and unary `-` fail dispatch under walk. Under walk, an inferred element type is a run-time class, so they give a plain array (row 721). Write the static argument.

**Arguments convert by declared coercions, and a generic call promotes.** Walk converts at a call, a typed binding and an assignment, and chooses the coercion by the run-time value; the checker chooses it statically (P-59). Promotion instantiates a generic declaration at the narrowest type into which all its arguments coerce (P-74). So `f[\T\](a: T, b: T)` on a `ZZ32` and a `ZZ64` runs at `ZZ64`. Walk does not promote the elements of a tuple or varargs: it takes their join (rows 395, 511). Where several declarations apply only by coercion and none is more specific, both paths stop: "Ambiguous coercion". Where the tied declarations differ only at the positions of the call's numerals, the checker reads the numeral as `ZZ32`, or `ZZ64` or `ZZ` where the value does not fit.

**An integer converts to another integer type by a checked getter or by a low-bits function (P-161).** To convert a value, write a getter, as `x.asZZ32`: `asZZ32`, `asZZ64`, `asNN32`, `asNN64` or `asZZ`. It keeps the value or raises `IntegerOverflow`. The low-bits functions `narrow`, `widen`, `signed`, `unsigned` and `big` keep the low bits and never raise, as Java's `(int)` does. On the fixed-width types, `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32` and `NN64`, `narrow` and `widen` give the 32-bit and the 64-bit type of the same sign, `signed` and `unsigned` the signed and the unsigned type of the same width, and `big` a `ZZ`. So `narrow` of a `ZZ64` outside `ZZ32`'s range wraps silently. In the interpreter's library, each fixed-width type has all five functions, and one that keeps the type returns the value, as `widen` of a `ZZ64`. `ZZ` has only `big`, so for a `ZZ` value `z`, `narrow(z)` finds no declaration: write `z.asZZ32`. Each `bitsAs…` getter equals `unsigned` or `signed`, as `bitsAsNN32` of a `ZZ32`. Until the switch-over, the compiler's prelude has only these getters: `asZZ` on each fixed-width type, `asZZ32` on `ZZ32` and `ZZ64`, `asNN32` on `NN32`, and `asNN64` on `NN64`. It has no `big`, and of the low-bits functions only those that change the type, as `narrow` of a `ZZ64` (row 349).

**`Number` declares nothing (P-165).** Each of the eight number types, and `IntLiteral`, declares its own `asFloat` into `RR64`. So generic code over `T extends Number` can call on a `T` no method or operator that the number types declare, `asFloat` among them. Two numbers of different types compare by `=` only where a coercion carries one into the other: the library declares `=` for each such pair, so a `ZZ32` and a `ZZ64` of equal value are `=`. Otherwise `=` is `SEQV` ("Traits and objects"), and answers `false` without an error: `1/2 = 0.5` is `false`, as is a `ZZ64` against an equal `RR64`. To compare values across types at known types, write `asFloat(x) = y`. In generic code over `T extends Number`, declare your function once for each number type instead. A program may also declare its own number type below `Number` (P-160).

**An integer power answers its base's type (P-153).** In the interpreter's library, `^` takes an exponent of any integer type. At a negative exponent, 1 and -1 give their power, 0 raises `DivisionByZero`, and other bases raise `IntegerOverflow`. For a result that is not an integer, write `2.0^(-1)`, or a `QQ` base as `(2/3)^(-1)`, not `10^(-k)`. Until the switch-over, the compiler's library has integer powers only at `ZZ32`, `NN32` and `NN64`, each with an exponent of its own type; its `RR64` power takes an `RR64` or a `ZZ32` exponent, a negative one included. Its `ZZ32` power gives 0 at a negative exponent for other bases. At a base of 0 it throws a Java exception that no `catch` sees (rows 441, 523).

**`/` on two integers answers a `QQ`.** So `7 / 2` is `7/2`, not 3. Truncate with `DIV`, on both paths. `DIV` answers its operands' type and rounds toward zero. For a float, make one operand a float, as `(1.0 s) / n` for `ZZ32` values `s` and `n`. Convert each `ZZ64` operand with `asFloat`, as `asFloat(s) / asFloat(n)`. Until the switch-over, the compiler's library has no `QQ` and declares `/` only at `RR64`, so a compiled `7 / 2` is a static error.

## Reductions and comprehensions

A clause form is a reduction or comprehension with generators in brackets, as `SUM[j <- 0#n] f(j)`.

**A reduction's static argument depends on the path.** The checker does not infer it for `SUM`, `PROD`, `BIG MAX` and `BIG MIN`, whose bound names the parameter (row 731). Write it in every clause form, as `SUM[\ZZ32\][j <- 0#n] f(j)`. Other reductions take their bound, or the expected type where the bound does not fit. Walk instantiates a reduction at its value's declared type: a local variable's, or a top-level or local function's return type, also where the clause form ends a block. A method's return type, a field, a top-level variable, a parameter and an assignment do not direct it. Else walk takes the join of the elements' run-time types. If that join is outside the reduction's bound, each `+` runs at its operands' types. An element that does not convert to the instance stops in `__bigOperator`, "body param 1". Departures under walk:

- with no declared type, an empty `SUM` gives the integer 0 (row 716);
- a comprehension inside another clause form is built at its elements' run-time types (rows 20, 717);
- a written static argument that is not a number type ends an empty `SUM` in `CastError` (row 436).

**A reduction without an identity lifts its elements to `Maybe[\R\]` inside the reduction.** `BIG MIN`, `BIG MAX` and the string reduction `BIG //` extend `AssociativeReduction[\R\]`, whose `simpleJoin` takes and answers `R`. `BIG MAX` over a generator still answers `R`. Walk refuses at load a reduction without static parameters that declares `simpleJoin` at `Any` or untyped. A generic one stops at its first join. The team's tests declare `simpleJoin` so: do not copy them.

## Implementation limits

**Walk has no static types.** Walk will run the checker only after the switch-over (P-12). So walk runs programs that the checker refuses. Besides a `Boolean`, it takes a `Maybe` as an `if` condition, `Just` as true and `Nothing` as false. It refuses any other value. The specification and the checker take only a `Boolean`, so do not write a `Maybe` condition. The compiled path's own limits are in `compiler.md`.

**Write every parameter type.** The compiled path refuses a parameter without a type, of a function, a method or a local function: "Missing parameter type for". Walk runs it, except in a method that implements an abstract one (row 405). A component's function that leaves out its return type takes the api's declaration at its parameter types. With none or several, the checker types the body.

<!-- What Pavol, the curator, knows, graded by topic, for pitching an explanation or an ask at him, with each line's evidence in PROFILE-sources.md beside it. -->

# What Pavol knows

A topic reads `topic — level — how to pitch it`. `1 → 3` is a level that rose: pitch at the later one.

- 4, expert: hands-on depth; talk as to a peer.
- 3, working: uses it correctly; no explanation, define only the project's own terms.
- 2, familiar: knows the idea, not the details; a one-line reminder before it is used.
- 1, heard of: knows the name; explain it with one concrete case before using it.
- 0, new: explain from the ground up, concrete cases first, with the shortest grounding that worked where there is one.

## Topics

### Languages and tools

- Benchmarking and measurement statistics — 4 — talk as to a peer; frame speed results this way.
- Swift as a library and benchmark writer — 3 — his first frame; its compiler's insides, and its names for unique references and copy-on-write, are 1.
- Scala (2.8 era), Java and the JVM, Python, iOS, as a user — 3 — take as known; their compilers' insides are new.
- Rust, Julia, Kotlin, Clojure, C++ templates — 2 — one line on the peer's idea; Clojure's multimethods are 1.
- What generators cost against a loop — 3 — he measured it himself; use it for big operators.
- APL — 0 — the side quest is closed.

### Types and language design

- Type theory, formally — 0 — a concrete Fortress program and several cases before any rule.
- Dispatch on all arguments; exclusions; coercion against subtyping; `Any` against `Object` — 1 → 3 — take as known.
- The checker's overload rules — 1 — the idea stuck, the rules didn't; show concrete pairs of declarations.
- Erased against kept generics; traits that give behavior; a subtype with its own operation — 3 — he judges by ergonomics and reuse, not purity.
- `where` clauses; soundness — 0 → 2 — remind him that `where` narrows where a declaration applies.
- `nat` size parameters — 0 → 2 — remind him that a `nat` is a size the type carries; arithmetic on sizes is 0.
- An interface against a trait — 1 — he is unsure of the words; say "extends".

### Mathematics

- Matrix and vector products, the dot product — 1 — he knows only that inner dimensions match; start from a 2×2 matrix times a vector, show that order matters, then C4's shapes: 16×16 (attention), 27×16 (token table), 64×16 (feed-forward).
- Rings, fields, additive groups — 0 — no grounding has worked yet.
- Identity elements on each type's algebra — 3 — take as known.
- Q, Z and N; `ZZ` signed, `NN` not — 0 → 3 — take as known.
- The library's number types — 2 — bottom up, `ZZ32` first; top down failed.
- Floating point — 2 — he knows IEEE rounding against Java's; infinities among the rationals were new.
- Reshape, ravel, outer product, tensor — 0 — define each on a small array.
- Mathematical notation — 1 — set it beside the Fortress code that computes it.

### Machine learning

- micrograd, microGPT, nanoGPT; FP32; integer tokens — 3 — take as known; microGPT's baseline is CPython or NumPy.
- KV cache, loss curves, early stopping, Chinchilla — 2 — a one-line reminder.
- Backpropagation, functional or tape-style, and its cost — 1 — his views are guesses.
- Big operators as ML papers write them — 1 — "hardly a yardstick", he says.
- Attention and softmax — 0 — learning them was microGPT's point for him; teach from C4's code.

### Fortress, its sources and the record

- Steele's talks: juxtaposition, undefined precedence, parallel loops, inference, units, `Σ` over new types — 3 — take as known.
- Where intent lives: the papers, the TeX not the PDF, the team's later word, the library among the sources — 3 — his rules.
- Who did what: Ryu's front end, Park's POPL 2019 paper — 3 — take as known.
- The library's shape: `Vector` and `Matrix` for numbers only — 2 — a one-line reminder.
- The specification, the papers, the library's text — 1 — unread; quote the line that decides.
- Reading Fortress code — 1 → 2 — he reads a declaration line by line; gloss each new construct.
- `label` and `exit`, `comprises`, `atomic`, `thrower`, `reflect`, DSL blocks, where whitespace counts — 0 — one concrete case each.
- FACTS, POSITIONS, the original protocol — 0 — never read; say what an entry says.
- Walk against the compiled path; the compiler's prelude — 0 → 3 — take as known.

### Compilers and run times

- JVM performance: boxing, the JIT, specialization, unboxed doubles — 1 → 3 — where he grew most.
- The pipeline, the caches, JVM array limits, warm-up, races hidden by one thread — 3 — take as known.
- Loom, the Vector API, Truffle, GraalVM — 0 → 2 — a one-line reminder.
- The class loader and its descriptors — 0 → 2 — from his own picture: sizes stamped into a class, as Swift mangles names, so the JIT drops bounds checks.
- One-time facts: which phases run the checker, the earlier compiler, a coercion's cost at run time, a load of 30 — 1 — one line when it comes up.
- The checker count and the distance to the switch-over — 1 — each time: what each counts, and why one can jump.

### The repository and the process

- Git; Claude Code's client; test-first, with `XXX` tests until a fix flips them — 3 — take as known.
- The platform: remote sessions, secrets in a container, the weekly reset — 1 — one line when it matters.
- The project's own terms; his past rulings — 2 — he forgets them after a gap; restate them by content.
- POSITIONS, "History he knows", and his decisions — 3 — take as known; cite a decision by what it says, never by its number.
- The coordinator's three principles — 1 — he knows the nine-step form, not these.

## How to explain to him

- Pitch at a software engineer who directs the work, not a researcher. Say what a feature costs.
- Concrete cases before the rule: several, on C4 or a Fortress program. He checks them for a contradiction, then takes the rule.
- Frame in what he knows, his own analogies first: the complex-number Mandelbrot, the diagonal matrix, Swift's debug builds, LLVM's lit.
- Define each term where it is used.
- Show Fortress code as Fortress, infix, not calls. Set notation beside the code. Draw a picture where structure matters.
- An ask: the question, context with a primer, numbered options with trade-offs and none that does nothing, the ask, the recommendation last. On types: the specification and the team's later word first, then the library, then the peers as context only. Say what each option does for a fast microGPT.
- One ask at a time, answerable as "3b". Show the wording before a yes. Mark a decision surfaced for his learning as one.
- Length by mode: three lines and "holding" while he reads turn by turn; an ask 1.5K to 3.3K, 5K with a refresher; long only to establish facts, never unasked.
- If he answers a long turn piece by piece: hold, list his points, and wait.
- When he's tired: one item, a default he can take, an offer to come back to it.
- When he ends "how wrong am I?": answer it, and reflect his idea back refined.
- He reads fast and forgets: restate, don't refer back.
- Plain words, halfway to ASD-STE100, positive phrasing.
- The phone, with Speak: a Select button per section, links not paths, no tables, numbers as K and M. A stop can be an accidental tap.
- Dictation: repair a term silently unless two readings differ. Seen, as heard → meant: forty five → Fortify, contact → compact, WordPress → Fortress, Table → Fable, scalar → Scala, Perl → parallel, Docker → checker, time system → type system, rank → rung, net → nat, Sue → Hsu, Popple → POPL, 16 → 64.

## Words to avoid

- A bare label: "P1", "row 40", "answer 9", "the judge", "the line". Name the thing.
- "Closure" for the integer tower; "sealed" for `Σ`; "revising the specification" for reconciling its contradictions.
- "Tensor", "reshape", "ravel", "outer product", "ring", "field", undefined; "coercion" for "conversion".
- "Yesterday"; "we" for him and Claude; a coda, a slogan, a clever turn.

## Open contradictions

- Length: he demands short replies, yet praised a long one while facts were being established.
- Reading: he says he hasn't read the specification or the library, yet spot-checks them and recalls Steele's talks exactly.
- Type theory: he says he knows none, yet reasons soundly about coercion, bounds and erasure.
- Scala: he says it earned his Stack Overflow points; most of the account is iOS.
- Peers: he asks what they do, yet rules that they only decide between the designers' choices; "context only" is the record's reading.
- Ownership: he wants every choice, yet at times takes a default unread.
- History: he recalls `main` as free of the third-party port; the record says otherwise.
- Other languages: his claims about them are unchecked; check one before building on it.

171	  - 20 and 432: generics of float numerals made at `FloatLiteral`.
172	  - 364: generics at `Int` and `FlatString`.
173	  - 721 and 722: factories at `Int`.
174	  - 807: `assert` falls back to `SEQV`, so `assert(V("ab"), V("ab"), m)` fails under walk.

354	## Summary
355	
356	Each path turns a literal into a value by its own code. Walk makes a new `FString` for every evaluation of a string literal. It gives an integer numeral the class `Int`, `Long` or `BigNum` by its magnitude. It keeps a float numeral as a `FloatLiteral`, which carries its text. The compiled path wraps each string literal in a new `FJavaString`. It boxes numerals as `FIntLiteral` and `FFloatLiteral`, which the checker types as `IntLiteral` and `FloatLiteral`.
357	
358	How this meets equivalence:
359	- **Strings.** `"ab" SEQV "ab"` is `false` on both paths, even for one literal evaluated twice. `=` compares text. Generics are made at `FlatString` under walk and at `String` compiled. An empty string's `SEQV` depends on where it came from.
360	- **Integers.** Under walk `3 SEQV z` is `true`. Compiled it is `false`, which is the specification's answer.
361	- **Floats.** Under walk, `y: RR64 = 0.5` stays a `FloatLiteral`, so it is not `SEQV` a computed `0.5`, and neither are value objects that hold it. Compiled, it converts today. After the switch-over it will not, by reading, because the one library declares `FloatLiteral` below `RR64`. Walk prints a numeral's text, so two `SEQV` values print `2.5` and `2.50`. `q: QQ = 0.5` is refused.
362	
363	**Against the specification:**
364	- Float numerals are not converted at typed places (`literals.tex:132-148`).
365	- `QQ` does not coerce from a compound numeral.
366	- `SEQV` values print differently (`objects.tex:38-39`).
367	- Walk makes generics at `Int` (row 364).
368	
369	**`FloatLiteral` is not in the specification.** The revision gave compound numerals no type.
370	
371	**Against expectation, but not against the specification:**
372	- Literal strings are not `SEQV`. The text does not say whether a literal is one object, and "Literals are values; they do not require evaluation" leans toward one.
373	- `3 SEQV z` is `false` compiled.
374	
375	**New evidence.** The 2012 restart (`literals.tick:14-29`) says: "All literals represent value objects; therefore their values do not have object identity". It also says a numeral with a '.' is a `QQ`. No note of the record cites it.

377	**Changes 39, 41 and 42** record these representation choices as if the language gave them. In change 39, the literal-string sentence is placed beside the cases it says to assert as correct. Change 41's example rests on the float representation. Change 42 says no row holds the float `false`, while Appendix I calls it a departure. Change 40 records a walk defect, with its row. Changes 43 and 44 are not the pattern.

Sets already come out at the trait, because walk's recheck of an F-bound reads the supertypes (row 646). Lists do not.

Every one gives the target answer: `lk` picks the `List[ZZ32]` declaration, `SUM <|[\ZZ32\] 1,2,3|>` is 6, `Just[\ZZ32\](3) = Just[\ZZ32\](3)` is true, `openAt[\ZZ32\](z)` is an `OpenRange[\ZZ32\]`, the nested `BIG CONCAT` gives `<|2, 4, 6|>`, and the list `<` is true.

### 1. Where walk instantiates at a run-time class

**The source of the class.** `FValue.type()` of a `ZZ32` value is `value object Int extends ZZ32` (`LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fsi:127`), returned by `FNativeObject.java:38-40`. The traits pair with the objects as follows (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi`):
- `ZZ32 comprises { Int }` (`:551-553`)
- `ZZ64 comprises { Long }` (`:618-620`)
- `ZZ comprises { BigNum }` (`:686-688`)
- `NN64 comprises { UnsignedLong }` (`:495-497`)
- `RR64 comprises { Float, FloatLiteral }` (`:291-294`)

**The sites.**
1. **Generic functions, constructors and generic dotted methods.** All go through `EvaluatorBase.inferAndInstantiateGenericFunction` (`interpreter/evaluator/EvaluatorBase.java:72-94`). It reads the value's type at four places:
   - `FType at = a.type();` at `:602` (unmoved since d4d454f9d);
   - the varargs unification, `:606-611`;
   - the unification of a parameter type that mentions `T` inside it, `:634-637`;

2. **Reductions and comprehensions with no declared type.** `Evaluator.bigOperatorByElements` (`Evaluator.java:799-815`) calls `__elemsOf`. That builds each element with `__ElemsOne(x)` through `__elemsOne(x: Any)` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:1428`, object at `:1408`): a constructor inference from the class. `__elemsJoin` (`:1411`) joins them, and `EvaluatorBase.elementsType` (`:267-271`) hands the join to the big operator.
3. **List displays.** `opr <|[\E\] xs: E... |>` (`Library/List.fsi:114`) is a varargs inference (rows 20 and 432).
4. **The array factories and `openRange`.** `array1` and `array2` (`FortressLibrary.fss:2692-2703`) and `openRange` (`:4327-4332`) typecase over a witness that puts `T` inside an invariant generic. **Not a site.** An untyped array literal is refused: "Can't infer element type for array construction" (`LHSEvaluator.java:145`).

### 2. The ways (item 1)

**A. Inference reads a number value at its trait.** This is possible before the switch-over.

**B. Every instance is made at the trait, at the factories.**

### 3. What else still shows the five to a program (item 2)

**Error messages.** They print `FType.toString`, which is the class name (`types/FType.java:115-117`, `types/FTraitOrObject.java:183-191`).

| Message | Code | Measured output |

**Reflection.** `Reflect$ToString` returns `ty.toString()` (`glue/prim/Reflect.java:434-437`), and `typeOf` returns the run-time type (`:210-213`). `R364I` printed:

**Types a program names.** The five are nameable types:

- `NumberPrintTest.fss:32` and `:36` (a team test) have `BigNum` and `UnsignedLong` arms.

**Dispatch, bindings, `instanceOf`, factories, `SUM`.** These are in section 0. A and B fix them, except for `FloatLiteral` and strings.

**Already fixed** (F-328): `ilkName`, `asString` and `asDebugString` print the trait (`R364I` I6 prints "a VCell[\ZZ32\]: VCell[\ZZ32\]").

### 4. Conflicts with decisions (item 3)

- **P-12.** Its "not changed for this" is about running the checker. A, B, F and G give walk no static types, so none conflicts. - **P-59 and P-74.** No conflict: an `Int` value's coercions are `ZZ32`'s, and `narrowest` still gives `ZZ64` for a `ZZ32` with a `ZZ64` (by reading).

By reading, `<|"a","b"|>` is an `ArrayList[\FlatString\]`, and `FlatString` is no `StandardTotalOrder[\FlatString\]`. So once walk reads `List`'s `where { E extends StandardTotalOrder[\E\] }` (`List.fsi:69-70`), a display of string literals loses `<`. Row 774 needs S or P-12 as well.

### Decisions

- I counted `FloatLiteral` outside "the five", following the brief's list, F-328 and F-57.
- I treated the string half of row 364 as a separate sub-choice.
- Every effect of a fix is by reading; nothing was built.

### For FACTS

1. **The five are visible beyond dispatch and binding.** Under walk at `157323e5`, an instance inferred from a number value is at the class: `Just(3) = Just[\ZZ32\](3)` is false, `VCell(3) SEQV VCell[\ZZ32\](3)` is false, `instanceOf[\Cell[\ZZ32\]\](Cell(3))` is false, and `typeOf(3)` prints `Int`. 2. **Lists stay at the class while sets get the trait.** Displays and comprehensions with no declared type are `ArrayList[\Int\]`; sets are `NodeSet[\ZZ32\]`, through the F-bound recheck. Evidence: `R364J` J4 and J5.

4. **The team's library already works around this.** `Library/ReflectiveQuickCheck.fss:233-239` converts `Float` to `RR64` by hand for this reason.
5. **The record overstates how far the fix reached.** F-74 and F-328 stand, but messages and `typeOf` still print the class, and three revival tests pin `(Int,Int)` in their keys.

### Commands

`import Reflect.{...}` with `typeOf(x)` prints walk's own run-time type text, which `ilkName` hides since F-328.

### Questions for the curator (decisions not taken)

1. **Close row 364's number half now?** The options are A (one rung; respell `LongStringTests:121` and `:141` as `Generator⟦ZZ32⟧`), B (one rung; no team-test line; but it identifies two written types), F (typed bindings only), or G (keep writing the argument until E). A conflicts with no decision.
2. **Map `FloatLiteral` too?** It closes row 20's example and the float cases of 432 and 721, but splits walk from the checker.
3. **Map the library's string objects to `String` (S)?** It closes the asserted half of 364 and keeps string lists ordered once row 774's walk half lands.
4. **The message half.** Render the five by their trait in walk's error messages and in `Reflect$ToString`, and move the three `TupleOrder*Refused.test` keys, or leave the messages as they are?

### Summary (under 400 words)

**The gap.** Walk infers a static argument from `FValue.type()`, which is the class `Int`, `Long`, `BigNum`, `Float` or `UnsignedLong`. The reads are at `EvaluatorBase.java:602`, `:645` (`narrowest`, candidates `:782-785`) and `:936`. Generic calls, constructors, dotted methods, list displays (varargs) and comprehensions (`__ElemsOne`) all take that path. Sets already get the trait, through the F-bound recheck. The array factories and `openRange` then fail through their witness (rows 721, 722).

**Visible to a program today** (measured at `157323e5`):
- dispatch past `Cell[\ZZ32\]`, typed-binding refusals, and `typecase` and `instanceOf` misses;
- `Just(3) = Just[\ZZ32\](3)` is false, and `typeOf(3)` prints `Int`;
- messages such as "RHS expression type Int…", "got arg 3: ZZ32 of type Int" and "args = (Cell[\Int\])";
- `typecase` arms that name the five.

**The ways.**
- **A**, reading the five at their trait in inference, is about 40-50 lines in 3 files and one walk rung. It closes 364's number half, 721 and 722, and the integer cases of 717, 432, 20 and 824, and four expected-failure tests flip. It breaks the team's `LongStringTests` (`Generator⟦Int⟧` at `:121` and `:141`).
- **B**, canonicalizing at the four instance factories, is about 50-70 lines in 6 files and one rung. It reaches the same rows and changes no team-test line, but it identifies two types a program can name, against `types-vals-vars.tex:51-52`.
- **C** and **D** are large and against the specification or F-74 and P-169.
- **E** (P-12 with P-76) gives `Cell(z)` `ZZ32` from the checker, but `Cell(3)` becomes `Cell[\IntLiteral\]`. A or B remains useful after it.
- **F** (expected type, row 510) fixes typed bindings only. **G** is writing the argument.

**microGPT.** No line of either program builds a generic from a numeral or a number value; no way except D changes them.

**Conflicts.** None with a decision for A. P-48's "the value's type" needs your reading. P-154's condition for row 774 is met for integer lists only: string-literal lists, `List[\FlatString\]`, would lose `<` unless strings are mapped too.

**Open.** `FloatLiteral` (mapping it would split walk from the checker), strings, and the message half, which three revival tests pin.

content.content:
usage: facts-extract.sh [--check] [--part N] [--page-bytes N] [--root DIR] [--common] [QUERY ...]

Prints what the queries name, whole and in the order they are given; a rung's
briefing is one such command. Each piece comes under a line naming its file
and section. The output comes in parts of at most PAGE_BYTES (default 28000);
part 1 opens with the size of the whole output in bytes and estimated tokens,
then what was asked for, where it is and what was not found; each part says
whether there is a next one, and --part N prints part N.

QUERY is one of:
  F-87, P-48             the entry of that number in FACTS.md or POSITIONS.md
  F-87+                  the entry, then each entry it points to and each entry
                         that points to it, each once, one level
  history:F-87           the entry's blocks in FACTS-history.md or
                         POSITIONS-history.md, oldest first: the provenance line
                         of each change and the line it replaced
  TITLE                  the FACTS.md entry whose title holds TITLE: an entry's
                         title is its bold opening, or where it has none, its
                         opening words up to the first colon, semicolon or full
                         stop; when no current title holds it, the entry one of
                         whose former titles (in FACTS-history.md) does, with a
                         line saying it was retitled
  section:HEADING        every entry of the FACTS.md section whose heading holds HEADING
  index:WORDS            the INDEX.md lines that hold every one of WORDS (at most 10)
  ledger:ROW             row ROW of the gap ledger, whole, under its section and
                         the table's header
  ledger-find:WORDS      one line for each gap ledger row that holds every one of

# Strings under `SEQV`: value or reference, for the curator's decision

The tree is `main` at `a959ab2aa`. Its build is current: `ProjectFortress/build/implementation.stamp` and `default_repository/caches/implementation.stamp` both read `180a6844e44e…`. Every program below is a scratch file under `tmp/streqv/`, not committed. Each point quotes its output. A Java path without a prefix is under `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/`.

## 1. The question and a primer

**The question.** Is `"ab" SEQV "ab"` true for two strings built apart? If yes, strings are value objects under `SEQV`. If no, they are reference objects.

**The words.**

1. *`SEQV`* is strict equivalence, also called object equivalence. Its symbol is ≣, U+2263, "strictly equivalent to". `SEQV` and `===` are its ASCII spellings (`parser/Literal.rats:303`; `parser_util/precedence_resolver/Operators.java:2109`). Note: it is not ≡, U+2261. The parser reads `EQV` and `EQUIV` as ≡, a different operator (`Literal.rats:301-302`).
2. *Value object*: an object with no identity. Two of them built apart can be the same. *Reference object*: an object with an identity. Two of them built apart are always different.
3. *Walk* is the interpreter. The *compiled path* compiles to JVM bytecode. Each has its own library today. The compiled one is the *prelude*. At the *switch-over* the compiled path moves onto walk's library, and the prelude goes (`.claude/skills/fortress-repo/SKILL.md`, "The phases").
4. A *flat string* is one Java string (`object FlatString`). A *rope* is a tree of strings (`object CatString`). A *substring* is a view into another string (`object SubString`).

**The specification's rule.** `Specification/basic/objects.tex:424-445`, "Object Equivalence":

> The trait Any declares the object equivalence operator ≣. This operator is automatically defined for all objects; it is a static error for the programmer to override it.

So `SEQV` is the one comparison that every value has. A program may not override it. The rule, in short:

- Different dynamic types, "including the instantiations of all static parameters": always false.
- Two value objects of one type: true "if and only if corresponding fields of the objects are themselves equivalent"; "two binary words are strictly equivalent if and only if they contain the same bit pattern" (so floats by their bits).
- Two references: true "if and only if the two object references refer to the identical reference object".
- Two functions: true only if they behave alike, and "the fortress implementation is free to return false".

**Which objects are value objects.** `objects.tex:22-31`: an object is "a reference object if it has an object trait type that is not declared with the `value` modifier", and a value object if it is a tuple, `()`, or declared `value`. The section "Value Objects" (`:347-422`) defines the modifier.

**The chapter's opening line.** `objects.tex:15`: "Value objects and properties are not yet supported."

**Why strings are the open kind.** The examples name booleans, numeric literals, floats and integers as value objects (`:39-43`). They name "arbitrary-precision numbers and aggregates such as arrays, lists and sets" as reference objects (`:52-54`). They never name strings. Just before that list the text asks itself: "What about reference objects that have no mutable fields?" (`:51`). Strings are exactly that kind.

## 2. The library's declarations

| Declaration | File and line | `value`? |
|---|---|---|
| `trait String` | `Library/FortressLibrary.fss:4341`, `.fsi:2447` | no |
| `object FlatString` | `Library/FlatString.fss:34`, `.fsi:16` | no |
| `object CatString(first, second)` | `Library/String.fss:75`, `.fsi:25` | no |
| `object SubString(baseString, range)` | `Library/String.fss:353`, `.fsi:34` | no |
| `value object EmptyString` | `Library/String.fss:282`, `.fsi:28` | yes |

So the library is split. Its empty string is a value object. Its other three are reference objects by the specification's definition.

**How a string's `=` is defined.**

1. `FlatString` declares `opr =(self, other: FlatString)` on the glue class `FlatString$Eq` (`FlatString.fss:70-71`). That class is Java's `self.equals(other)`, text equality (`interpreter/glue/prim/FlatString.java:131-136`). Its `<`, `>`, `CMP` use `cmp`, the helper `stringOps.compareTo` (`FlatString.fss:72-76`, `:85-86`).
2. `trait String` declares no `=` itself. It declares `CMP` character by character (`FortressLibrary.fss:4368-4369`). It inherits `=` from `StandardPartialOrder`: `opr =(self, other:T) = EqualTo = (self CMP other)` (`:232`). That is text equality for any two strings, of any shape.
3. There is no top-level `=` over `(String, String)` in walk's library (a grep for `opr =(` with `String` finds only `FlatString.fss:70` and `CaseInsensitiveString.fss:30`).
4. The fallback `opr =(a:Any, b:Any) = a SEQV b` (`FortressLibrary.fss:96`) and `Equality`'s `= ... self SEQV other` (`:101`) never see two strings: `StandardPartialOrder`'s `=` is more specific.

**Strings are immutable.** The string objects declare no `var` field (the `var`s in `String.fss` belong to `BalancingForest`, `:185-186`, `StringStats`, `:510-514`, and locals). The specification lists `String` with `Character` and the numerals among the "simple standard types for literals", and says "Values of these types are immutable" (`Specification/basic/types-vals-vars.tex:572-581`).

## 3. What each runtime does today

**Walk's code.** `interpreter/evaluator/values/FString.java:35-38`:

Compiled today it prints `PASS 'cat'==='cat'` and `PASS 'cat' NEQV 'dog'`, 'run rc=0'. Under walk it stops at load, 'Operator NEQV is not defined.' ## 4. The team's sources and which way they point

1. **The specification.** It is silent on strings. Read literally, `object FlatString` without `value` is a reference object, so `"ab" SEQV ("a" || "b")` is false. But the chapter says value objects are "not yet supported" (`objects.tex:15`), and it leaves open "reference objects that have no mutable fields" (`:51`). It groups `String` with `Character` and the numerals as immutable values of literals (`types-vals-vars.tex:572-581`). The team's later restart, `Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/values.tick:39-56`, defines value and reference objects and does not name strings.
2. **Walk's library and code, 2008.** Text, for flat strings, from the first `SEQV` (`d56a402b4`) and in `FString.seqv` (`cd41f90eb`). Ropes and substrings fall to the object rule and get identity. No commit or comment says that ropes should differ from flat strings. The split comes from where the rope class lives, not from a stated rule. It makes `SEQV` change at `maxLeafSize`, a tuning variable.
3. **The prelude, 2010 to 2012.** Text: one overload of `===` over `(String, String)`, from 2010 to the team's last commit, by the compiled path's main author (`research/authorship.md:88`). The 2010 regression test asserts it. This is the team's later word (P-26). One limit: the family sits under "(* This is incomplete *)". P-26 says that code its author called a stub serves only the implementation. The note marks missing cases, which `equality.java:15` names: "tuples, value types". It does not mark the `String` line as a stub, and a test pins that line.
4. **Do they agree?** Yes, where the team wrote code for strings: both paths compare strings by their text. The only reading for identity is the specification's literal one, at a kind it does not name. The rope case under walk is the default of the object rule, not a team choice.

## 5. The peers, as context

Context only. Python, Java and Scala were run here (`tmp/streqv/`); the rest is from general knowledge, not run.

- **Swift.** `String` is a struct, a value type. `==` compares the text. `===` takes only class references, so a string has no identity.
- **Python.** `==` compares text. `is` compares identity, and its answer on equal strings depends on interning. Run: `py == : True  is : False`, with 'SyntaxWarning: "is" with 'str' literal. Did you mean "=="?'.
- **Haskell.** No identity at all. `String` is a list of `Char`; `==` is structural.
- **Java.** `==` on strings is identity, the known trap. Literals are interned, so two equal literals are `==`; a string built at run time is not. Run: `java ==: literal,literal true; literal,built false; equals true; intern true`.
- **Scala.** `==` calls `equals`, text. `eq` is identity. Run with the tree's Scala 2.13.18: `scala == true; eq false`.
- **Julia.** `String` is immutable. `===` on two equal strings is true: Julia compares strings by content, as it does other immutable values.

So the languages whose strict comparison means "no program can tell them apart" (Swift, Haskell, Julia) treat strings as values. Identity on strings survives only as Java's `==` and Python's `is`, both warned against.

## 6. What hangs on it in the tree

1. **microGPT.** `grep -c 'SEQV\|≡\|≣\|==='` over `explorations/run-c4/src/*.fs?` and `explorations/apl/mg/*.fs?` prints 0 for every file. The model compares strings, where it does, by `=`, which does not reach `SEQV` (section 2, point 4).
2. **`=` on strings.** Unchanged under either way: it is `CMP`, by text (section 2). Tuples have their own `=` element by element (`FortressLibrary.fss:4668`, `:4724`). Walk run `tmp/streqv/StrTupWalk.fss`: `1 tuple = flat: true rope: true =/=: false` and `2 assert passed`, 'rc=0'.
3. **The fallback `=`** at `FortressLibrary.fss:96` and `Equality`'s at `:101`: reached by a string only beside a non-string, where `SEQV` is false under both ways (different types).
4. **`AnyMaybe`'s `=`** (`:1615`): `Just` (`:1640`) has its own `=`, `x=o.get` (`:1660`), so two `Just`s of strings compare by text under both ways.
5. **`Set` and `Map`.** `if self SEQV other then true` (`Library/Set.fss:353`, `:360`, `:367`; `Library/Map.fss:448`) is a shortcut before a full comparison. The meaning changes only how often it fires.
6. **`Avl`.** `if v SEQV vv then (self,d) else (replaceValue(v),d)` (`Library/Avl.fss:177-180`). Both branches keep `v`, the old value, so the meaning does not change the tree's contents. (That `replaceValue(v)` keeps the old value and not `vv` may be a defect; not probed here.)
7. **Inside walk's run time.** `SEQV` on a tuple or a value object compares its parts by `FValue.seqv` directly (`FTupleLike.java:78`; `FOrdinaryObject.java:54`), not by the library's operator. So a string inside a tuple gets the run time's answer, whatever the library declares (section 7, (a), point 3).
8. **Tests that would change.** A grep of every test folder for `SEQV`, `===` and `≣` beside a string finds only `compiler_regressions/seqv.fss:22` and `:25`. No gated test asserts `SEQV` on strings. Indirect routes (strings inside tuples or value objects compared by `SEQV`) were not measured over the suites.
    - Under (a): no existing test changes.
    - Under (b): `seqv.fss:22` fails. It is the team's test, and ungated. `sequivTest.fss` does not change on strings.

## 7. The two ways

### (a) Strings are value objects, compared by their text

1. **Library.** One declaration over `String`, as the prelude's family did: `opr SEQV(a: String, b: String): Boolean = a = b`, beside `FortressLibrary.fsi:2645` and `FortressLibrary.fss:4650-4651`. The checker's rule refuses `===` only inside a trait or an object (`parser_util/SyntaxChecker.java:253-256`); Ryu's TODO there wants no top-level definition "when we have a better magic". The library is the language's own text, so this is a definition, not a programmer's override.
2. **Measured, prototype A.** Copies of `FortressLibrary.fss` and `.fsi` in `tmp/streqv/proto/`, each with that one line added, read by walk ahead of the library. The program of section 3, with a line 12 added, printed:

    ```
    3 flat, rope: true =: true
    4 rope, rope, other shape: true =: true
    7 sub, sub built apart: true =: true
    9 EmptyString, EmptyString: true; EmptyString, "": true =: true
    10 tuples: true ropes in tuples: false
    12 as Any: true numbers: true pair: true
    rc=0
    ```

    Walk loaded the overload beside the one at `Any`, and chose it by run-time types, also through `Any` (line 12). The plain build printed `12 as Any: false numbers: true pair: true`.
3. **Its limit.** Line 10 stays false: walk's run time compares tuple parts by `FValue.seqv`, not by the library's operator (section 6, point 7). The rung must close this: either the run time's recursion calls the library's `SEQV`, or each run time compares any `String` by text itself. On the compiled path, the same holds for `equality.sEquiv` once it compares tuples (row 907).
4. **The `value` modifier: not added.** A rope's fields are its halves, `first` and `second`. Under the specification's field rule, two equal texts of different shapes would be inequivalent. Measured, prototype V: `value object CatString` in copies of `String.fss` and `.fsi` (`tmp/streqv/proto2/`): `V1 equal text, same shape built apart: true`, `V2 equal text, other shape: false`, 'rc=0'. The declaration over `String` answers by the text and avoids this. `EmptyString` keeps its `value`: it has no fields, so all empty strings agree.
5. **Specification.** In the revision form (P-96): one Appendix I entry. A `\revision` callout at "Object Equivalence" (`objects.tex:424-445`): two strings are strictly equivalent if and only if they hold the same characters in the same order, whatever objects hold them. A callout at the lists (`:39-54`): strings among the value objects, compared by their characters. P-166's revision of the same list lands in the same rung. The entry quotes `Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/objects.tex`, says what a return to (b) would need, and names this decision.
6. **Runtimes.** Walk: the library line; the recursion of point 3. Compiled: none until the switch-over (`CompilerLibrary.fss:68` already answers so); then the one library's line serves, and the prelude goes.
7. **Tests.** None change. Add one test on both paths: two flat strings built apart, a flat string against an equal rope, two ropes of different shapes, a substring, `EmptyString` against `""`, through `Any`, and inside a tuple.

### (b) Strings are reference objects, the literal reading

1. **Library.** Nothing. `EmptyString` stays `value` and fieldless, so every `EmptyString` is `SEQV` every other, while two flat `""`s are not (section 3, line 9).
2. **Specification.** One Appendix I entry and a callout at the list (`objects.tex:52-54`), naming strings among the reference objects, so that the text says what it means. No rule changes.
3. **Walk.** `FString.seqv` (`FString.java:35-38`) answers false; `AnyPrim.sequiv`'s identity test (`AnyPrim.java:24`) still makes a string equivalent to itself.
4. **Compiled.** Delete `CompilerLibrary.fss:68`. Strings then fall to `:63`, `equality.sEquiv`, `a == b`. That is Java's `==` on the wrapping objects: false even for two equal literals (section 3, `StrRefComp`, line 1), unlike Java's own interned literals.
5. **Tests.** `compiler_regressions/seqv.fss:22`, the team's test, would print `FAIL 'cat'==='cat'`; it is ungated. No gated test changes. Add one test on both paths that two equal strings built apart are not `SEQV`.

## 8. How they weigh

The coordinator skill's three principles: the team's later word (P-26), the library as the team wrote it, and the peers only where the first two split or are silent (`.claude/skills/coordinator/SKILL.md:95`).

1. **The team's later word.** The prelude, 2010 to 2012, compares strings by text, and a test of 2010 pins it. The specification's only ground for identity is its silence. The later restart is silent too. So the later word points to (a).
2. **The library as the team wrote it.** Walk compares flat strings by text, from 2008. Its identity for ropes is a fallout of the object rule, which makes `SEQV` change with a string's length; nothing in the team's text asks for that. Its one `value` declaration among the strings is `EmptyString`. So the library points to (a), with the rope case as a gap.
3. **The peers.** The first two agree, so the peers do not weigh. As context, Swift, Haskell and Julia agree with (a); only Java's `==` and Python's `is` give (b).
4. **Agreement.** The principles that speak point the same way. The fork is settled by them.
5. **Is it consequential?** By the skill's test (`.claude/skills/coordinator/SKILL.md:99-104`): it touches no model line (section 6, point 1), changes no value the model computes, and changes no `=`. It reverses no decision of the curator; its specification entry sits beside P-166's, in the same rung. It can be undone in one commit: one library line, one spec entry. So it is not consequential, and could land as a default on the review list.

## 9. Recommendation

Take (a): strings are value objects compared by their text, by one `opr SEQV(a: String, b: String)` in the one library, no `value` on `FlatString`, `CatString` or `SubString`, the specification's lists and "Object Equivalence" revised in the revision form with P-166's entry, and walk's run-time recursion brought to the same answer for strings inside tuples, under one test on both paths.

content.content:
\note{We need to check whether the various types and values defined in this section are still correct.}

\begin{Grammar}
\emph{LiteralExpr} &::=& \texttt{(} \texttt{)}\\
&$|$& \emph{NumericLiteralExpr}\\
&$|$& \emph{CharLiteralExpr}\\
&$|$& \emph{StringLiteralExpr}\\
\end{Grammar}

Fortress provides boolean literals, \TYP{()} literal, character literals,
string literals, and numeric literals.  Literals are values; they do not
require evaluation.

\note{From here, copied from F1.0$\beta$.}

The literal \VAR{false} has type
\EXP{\TYP{BooleanLiteral}\llbracket\VAR{false}\rrbracket}.
The literal \VAR{true} has type
\EXP{\TYP{BooleanLiteral}\llbracket\VAR{true}\rrbracket}.
\note{And these are the only values of those types.}

The literal \EXP{()} is the only value with type \TYP{()}.
Whether any given occurrence of \TYP{()} refers to the value \EXP{()} or
to the type \TYP{()} is determined by context.

A character literal has type \TYP{Character}.
Each character literal consists of an abstract character in
\unicode~\cite{Unicode},
enclosed in single quotation marks (for example, `\txt{a}', `\txt{A}',
`\txt{\$}', `\txt{$\alpha$}', `\txt{$\oplus$}').
\marginnote{This is not true: Character literals include ``\b'' and
``LATIN CAPITAL A'', which do not ``consist of'' an abstract character enclosed in
single quotation marks.  I think it's better to remove most of this discussion and
direct the reader to the relevant section of Lexical Structure.
This section should be about {\bf semantics} of literals:
their values and types.}
The single quotes may be either true typographical ``curly'' single quotation marks
or a pair of ordinary apostrophe characters (for example, \txt{'a'}, \txt{'A'}, \txt{'\$'}, \txt{'$\alpha$'}, \txt{'$\oplus$'}).
See \secref{preprocessing-character-literals} for a description of how names of
characters may be used rather than actual characters within character literals,
for example `\txt{APOSTROPHE}' and `\txt{GREEK\_CAPITAL\_LETTER\_GAMMA}'.

A string literal has type \TYP{String}.
Each string literal is a sequence of \unicode\ characters enclosed in double
quotation marks (for example,
``\txt{Hello, world!}'' or ``\txt{$\pi\thinspace r^2$}'').
\marginnote{Again, I think this paragraph should mostly be eliminated and replaced with a pointer to the relevant section of Lexical Structure.

Here's a sentence I wrote as a replacement:
``A string literal (i.e., a sequence of characters enclosed in double quotation marks---see Section 5.10 for details) has type String.''}
The double quotes may be either true typographical ``curly'' double  quotation marks
or a pair of ``neutral'' double-quote characters (for example,
\txt{"Hello, world!"} or \txt{"$\pi\thinspace r^2$"}).
\secref{preprocessing-string-literals} also describes how names of
characters may be used rather than actual characters within string literals.
One may also use the escape sequences \txt{{\char'134}b} and \txt{{\char'134}t}
and \txt{{\char'134}n} and \txt{{\char'134}f} and \txt{{\char'134}r} as described in \cite{JLS}.


\note{We may want to eliminate the distinction between simple and compound numerals,
and just distinguish them by whether they have a radix point or not, when necessary
(i.e., ``Numerals may have a radix point.'').  Again,
that distinction is primarily a syntactic one, and can be discussed there if appropriate.}
Numeric literals in Fortress are referred to as \emph{numerals},
corresponding to various expressible numbers.
Numerals may be either \emph{simple} or \emph{compound}
(as described in \secref{numerals}).

A numeral containing only digits (let $n$ be the number of digits)
has type \EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeral}\llbracket{}n,10,v\rrbracket} where $v$ is the value of the numeral
interpreted in radix ten.  If the numeral has no leading zeros, or is
the literal \EXP{0}, then it also has type \EXP{\TYP{Literal}\llbracket{}v\rrbracket}.
\note{Can the type \EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeral}\llbracket{}n, 10, v\rrbracket}
have any value other than what you get from evaluating the corresponding literal?

What is the relationship between \EXP{\TYP{Literal}\llbracket{}v\rrbracket}
and \EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeral}\llbracket{}n, 10, v\rrbracket}?

We need to describe the \TYP{Numeral} type hierarchy.
All the numeric/numeral types should be defined and their relations to each other given.
And a reference to where that is done should be appear in this section (probably at the beginning of the section).
}

\note{Ought we discuss digit-group separators here?
Or is that just part of lexical structure?
(I think we intend that a numeral consisting of digits and digit-group separators has
type \EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeral}\llbracket{}n,10,v\rrbracket}
for appropriate values of \VAR{n} and \VAR{v}.)}

A numeral containing only digits (let $n$ be the number of
digits) then an underscore, then a radix indicator (let $r$ be the
radix) has type \EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeralWithExplicitRadix}\llbracket{}n,r,v\rrbracket}
where $v$ is
the value of the $n$-digit numeral interpreted in radix $r$.

A numeral containing only digits (let $n$ be the total number
of digits) and a radix point (let $m$ be the number of digits after
the radix point) has type
\EXP{\TYP{RadixPointNumeral}\llbracket{}n,m,10,v\rrbracket} where $v$ is
the value of the numeral, with the radix point deleted,
interpreted in radix ten.

A numeral containing only digits (let $n$ be the total number
of digits) and a radix point (let $m$ be the number of digits after
the radix point), then an underscore, then a radix indicator (let $r$
be the radix) has the following type:
\begin{Fortress}
\EXP{\TYP{RadixPointNumeralWithExplicitRadix}\llbracket{}n,m,r,v\rrbracket}
\end{Fortress}
where $v$ is the value of the $n$-digit numeral, with the radix point
deleted, interpreted in radix $r$.

Every numeral also has type
\EXP{\TYP{Numeral}\llbracket{}n,m,r,v\rrbracket}
for appropriate values of \VAR{n}, \VAR{m}, \VAR{r}, and \VAR{v}.


Numerals are not directly converted to any of the number types
because, as in common mathematical usage,
we expect them to be polymorphic.
For example, consider the numeral \EXP{3.1415926535897932384};
converting it immediately to a floating-point number
may lose precision.
If that numeral is used in an expression
involving floating-point intervals,
it would be better to convert it directly to an interval.
Therefore, numerals have their own types as described above.
This approach allows library designers to decide how numerals should
interact with other types of objects by defining coercion operations
(see \secref{coercion} for an explanation of coercion
in Fortress).
\Library\ define coercions
from numerals to integers (for simple numerals)
and rational numbers (for compound numerals).


\marginnote{What is an ``integer'' in this context?}
In Fortress, dividing two integers using the $/$ operator produces
a \emph{rational number};\marginnote{Not if the second integer is 0.}
this is true regardless of whether
the integers are of type $\mathbb{Z}$ (or \txt{ZZ}),
$\mathbb{Z}64$ (or \txt{ZZ64}), $\mathbb{N}32$ (or \txt{NN32}), or
whatever.  Addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division of rationals
are always exact; thus values such as \EXP{1/3} are represented exactly in
Fortress.

\note{We should give an example with a radix specifier.}
Numerals containing a radix point are actually rational
literals; thus \EXP{3.125} has the rational value \EXP{3125/1000}.
The quotient of two integer literals is a static expression
(described in \secref{static-expr}) whose value is rational.
Similarly, a sequence of digits with a radix point followed by the symbol
$\times$ and an integer literal raised to an integer literal,
such as \EXP{6.0221415 \times 10^{23}}
is a static expression whose value is rational.
If such static expressions are mentioned as part of a floating-point
computation, the compiler performs the rational arithmetic exactly and then
converts the result to a floating-point value, thus incurring
at most one floating-point rounding error.
But in general rational computations may also be performed at run time,
not just at compile time.
\note{This specifies too much about the implementation:
I don't think we should mention a compiler at all, except perhaps as informal discussion.
In particular, wouldn't it be correct if this arithmetic were actually deferred and
performed exactly at run time?}


A rational number can be thought of as a pair of integers $p$ and $q$
that have been reduced to ``standard form in lowest terms'';
that is, $q > 0$ and there is no nonzero integer $k$
such that $p \over k$ and $q \over k$ are integers
and $\left| {p \over k} \right| + \left| {q \over k} \right|
	< \left| p \right| + \left| q \right|$.
The type $\mathbb{Q}$ includes all such rational numbers.

The type $\mathbb{Q}^*$ relaxes the requirement $q>0$ to $q \geq 0$ and
includes two extra values, \EXP{1/0} and \EXP{-1/0} (sometimes called ``the
infinite rational'' and ``the indefinite rational'').
\marginnote{Is there any subtyping or coercion relationship between \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} and
\EXP{\mathbb{Q}*}?
If \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} is a subtype of \EXP{\mathbb{Q}*}
then static checking would normally disallow the assignment,
so is this a relaxation to that rule?  If so, the static checker needs to know about it.}
If a value of type $\mathbb{Q}^*$ is assigned to a
variable of type $\mathbb{Q}$, a \TYP{DivisionByZero} is thrown
at run time if the value is \EXP{1/0} or \EXP{-1/0}.

One way to think about coercion is that if type \VAR{T} can be coerced
to type \VAR{U}, then a value of type \VAR{T} can be used to ``stand
in'' for a value of type \VAR{U} in a functional call, for example.  This is
different from actually \emph{being} of type \VAR{U}; it means only
that, given any value of type \VAR{T}, an appropriate value of type
\VAR{U} can be computed to substitute for it.  Also, coercion occurs
only when the declared type of the corresponding parameter in the
functional declaration is exactly the type \VAR{U} being coerced to

 \VAR{T} can be coerced to type \VAR{U} then any subtype of \VAR{T}
 can also be coerced to type \VAR{U}.

where the context expects the expression to have type \VAR{U} and

\section{A Numeral Whose Conversions Tie}
\seclabel{numeral-default}

A numeral has a type of its own, from which \library\ define coercions to the
number types (\secref{literals}).
Where the types to which a numeral can be converted are incomparable under
$\morespecificeq$, as \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} and \EXP{\mathbb{N}32} are, each
taking a numeral and neither converting into the other, the numeral is read as
a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, or as a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} or a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} when its
value does not fit in the narrower type.
This holds in either step: in the choice among declarations that are applicable
to the call only with coercion and that the numeral would otherwise leave tied,
and in the instantiation of a type parameter that only numerals fix.
So of the declarations \EXP{g(x\COLON\mathbb{N}32)} and
\EXP{g(x\COLON\mathbb{Z}32)}, the call \EXP{g(0)} invokes the second; and a
type parameter that only numerals fix, whose bounds \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} and
\EXP{\mathbb{N}32} satisfy and the numeral's own type does not, is
instantiated at \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} when \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} holds the numerals'
values.

The rule settles only a tie that a numeral makes.
Where an argument that is not a numeral leaves the declarations applicable to a
call only with coercion tied, no declaration is the most specific, and the call
is a static error.

content.content:
\note{Properties are not yet supported. Of value objects, only strict
equivalence is supported: the interpreter and the compiled code compare two
value objects of one type field by field (\secref{equivalence}).}

\emph{Objects} are values that have \objecttypes\ described in
\secref{object-traits}.
Objects contain \emph{methods} (described in \secref{methods}) and
\emph{fields} (described in \secref{fields}).

An object is a \emph{value object}, a \emph{reference object},
or a \emph{function object}:
It is a function object if it has an arrow type,
a reference object if it has an object trait type
that is not declared with the \KWD{value} modifier
(see \secref{value-objects}),
and a value object otherwise
(i.e., if it has a tuple type, the type (),
or an object trait type declared
with the \KWD{value} modifier).

A value object cannot have mutable fields,
and it is completely determined by its type,
environment and its fields:
Value objects with the same type, environment and fields
are indistinguishable.
Thus, an implementation may freely copy value objects.
Most objects with simple standard types,
such as booleans,
numeric literals,
IEEE floating-point numbers,
integers of every precision,
and rational numbers are value objects.
%
In contrast,
reference objects are thought to ``reside in memory'',
and are identified by an \emph{object reference}.
A new object reference is created
whenever a reference object is constructed,
so that reference objects constructed separately are always distinct.
What about reference objects that have no mutable fields?
Reference objects include
strings
and aggregates such as arrays, lists and sets.
\revision{revival-object-kinds}{The Working Draft of February 2011 named
arbitrary-precision numbers among the reference objects and gave strings no
kind.
The revival decided on 6~November 2026 that the values of the
arbitrary-precision integer and rational types are value objects, as \library\
declare them, and on 6 and 7~November 2026 that strings are reference objects:
two strings are strictly equivalent only when they are one object, and their
text equality is their \EXP{=}.}
%
Function objects are immutable and have no fields.  Identity is not
well-defined for function objects, and attempting to check whether two
functions are equivalent returns an approximate result.
\secref{equivalence} describes object equivalence in further detail.

\subsection{Which objects are value objects}
\seclabel{revival-object-kinds}

\begin{description}
\item[Affected section] The opening section of \chapref{objects}, its list of
the kinds of objects.
\item[Change] Its sentence on the value objects named booleans, numeric
literals, IEEE floating-point numbers and integers; it now names integers of
every precision and rational numbers too.
Its sentence on the reference objects named arbitrary-precision numbers and
aggregates such as arrays, lists and sets; it now names strings and the
aggregates.
The passage gains one box.
The rule of strict equivalence (\secref{equivalence}) is unchanged: values of
different types are never strictly equivalent, value objects of one type are
when their fields are, a binary word by its bit pattern, and reference objects
only when they are one object.
\item[Rationale] This change does not follow from route~A; it follows two
decisions of the revival.
By the first, of 6~November 2026, the values of the arbitrary-precision integer
and rational types are value objects: \library\ declare the arbitrary-precision
integer as a value object, and the sentence's own list called integers value
objects and arbitrary-precision numbers reference objects, so the text
disagreed with itself and with the library; the library's declaration is the
deliberate word.
By the second, of 6 and 7~November 2026, strictly equivalent means the rule of
\secref{equivalence} on both implementations, with no special case for any type,
and strings are reference objects: \library\ declare every kind of string as an
object without the \KWD{value} modifier, so two strings are strictly equivalent
only when they are one object, and their text equality is their own \EXP{=}.
The Working Draft of February 2011 named no kind for strings, and the
team's implementations compared two flat strings by their text and two ropes
by identity.
The full reasoning is in
\nolinkurl{explorations/reviews/any-carrier-2026-11-06.md}, section~2.4, and
\nolinkurl{explorations/reviews/string-equivalence-2026-11-06.md} in the
revival's repository.
\item[Effect] Both implementations answer \EXP{\sequiv} by the rule, and both
read the \KWD{value} modifier.
\Library\ declare the rational type's object and the two numeral objects of the
interpreter as value objects.
The departures:
the interpreter gives a floating-point numeral bound to a variable of type
\EXP{\mathbb{R}64} the type of the numeral object, so it is not strictly
equivalent to a computed \EXP{\mathbb{R}64} value of the same bits;
an integer numeral is a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} or
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}} value in the interpreter, by its magnitude, and a numeral
object to the compiled type checker, so a numeral
compared with a typed value can answer differently on the two paths;
the compiled path's own library, used until the one library replaces it,
answers \EXP{\sequiv} on values of \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64},
\EXP{\mathbb{R}32} and \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}, on strings and on booleans by
\EXP{=} before it
reaches the rule, so there two equal strings built apart are strictly
equivalent and \EXP{0.0} is strictly equivalent to \EXP{-0.0} (row~908 of the
revival's gap ledger);
and \library\ declare \EXP{=} on pairs and triples only, so two tuples of four
or more elements are equal only when they are strictly equivalent, and two such
tuples of equal strings built apart are not equal (row~923 of the revival's
gap ledger).
The answers are gated by \nolinkurl{ProjectFortress/tests/StrictEquivalenceRuleWalk.fss},

helper, by \nolinkurl{ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/StrictEquivalenceRuleCompiled.fss}.
